passages.original: et gaudeo quod obscurissimas liber Zachariae pro- phetae, et inter duodecim longissimus, eo tempore disserendus est, quo ob festinationem ejus qui re- versurus est, nullam moram patitur interpretatio : sed velim nolim, saltem lucrativis per noctem horis atque furtivis dictare compellor, quod tibi dirigam. Scripsit in hunc prophetam Origenes duo volumina, usque ad tertiam partem libri a principio. Hippo- lytus quoque edidit Commentarios, et Didymus quoque Explanationum libros, me rogante, dictavit, quos cum aliis tribus 3 in Osee et mihi icpose- φώνησβν : sed tota eorum έζήγηαις allegorica fuit, et historiae vix pauca tetigerunt.
passages.english: And I am glad that the book of the prophet Zechariah, most obscure and the longest among the Twelve, has to be expounded at a time when, because of the haste of the one who is about to return, the interpretation allows no delay; but whether I will or not, I am compelled to dictate, at least in hours gained and stolen during the night, what I may send to you. Origen wrote two volumes on this prophet, reaching to the third part of the book from the beginning. Hippolytus also published Commentaries, and Didymus too dictated books of Explanations at my request, which, together with three others on Hosea, he dedicated to me as well; but their whole exposition was allegorical, and they barely touched on a few points of the history.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by the scan: 'icpose- φώνησβν' read as προσεφώνησεν ('dedicated, addressed'), and 'έζήγηαις' as ἐξήγησις ('exposition'). 'The one who is about to return' is not identified in the passage; it presumably refers to the bearer of the work.

passages.original: Possumus quatuor cornua, quae regnaverunt contra populum Dei, et quatuor πάθη accipere, quae eruditi non verbum de verbo exprimentes χακοζήλωςpassiones, sed perturbatio- nes interpretantur, aegritudinem animi et gau- dium : 792 duo praesentia, et duo futura, metum et cupiditatem, de quibus et illustris poeta signi- ficat (AEneid.VI) : Adversum has, quatuor fabri, et (ut ita dica.) medici, bonique artifices, non cernuntur a pro- pheta, necdum enim absque ostensione Dei per se eos videre poterat, sed ostenduntur ei a Domino, quatuor scilicet virtutes, prudentia, justitia, for- titudo, temperantia, de quibus plenissime in Offi- ciorum libris Tullius disputat, scribens proprium quoque de quatuor virtutibus librum. Qui ergo vitia destruunt, virtutes aedificant, omnesque san- cti, qui haec remedia possidentes instaurant sem- per Ecclesiam, fabri appellandi sunt.
passages.english: We can also take the four horns, which reigned against the people of God, as the four *pathē* [passions], which learned men, not rendering word for word in poor imitation as 'passions', translate as 'disturbances': distress of mind and joy, two [concerning] present [things], and two [concerning] future [things], fear and desire, which the illustrious poet also indicates (Aeneid 6). Against these, the four smiths, and (so to speak) physicians and good craftsmen, are not discerned by the prophet, for he could not yet see them by himself without God's showing, but they are shown to him by the Lord: namely the four virtues, prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, on which Tully [Cicero] discourses most fully in the books On Duties, also writing a separate book on the four virtues. Those, then, who destroy vices and build up virtues, and all the saints who, possessing these remedies, are always restoring the Church, are to be called smiths.
passages.notes: 'χακοζήλως' read as κακοζήλως ('in affected/poor imitation'). The Virgil quotation (Aeneid 6.733, 'hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice') appears to have dropped out of the text after 'significat'. 'ut ita dica.' read as 'ut ita dicam'.

Αlli enim Judaeorum putant jam haec ex parte completa a Zorobabel, usque ad C. Pom- peium, qui primus Romanorum Judaeam cepit et templum, quam historiam scribit Josephus. Alii autem, hoc est, 896 nos qui Christi censemur nomine, in Eccle- sia usque ad finem mundi quotidie expleri et ex- plenda, memoramus4.
passages.english: 7): 'Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man who cleaves to me, says the Lord of hosts: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' For some of the Jews think these things have already been partly fulfilled, from Zerubbabel up to Gnaeus Pompey, who was the first of the Romans to capture Judaea and the temple, a history which Josephus writes. Others, however, [think they] are to be fulfilled at the end of the world, when Jerusalem has been restored, which the wretched Jewish nation promises itself together with its *anointed one*, whom we read of above as the foolish shepherd. Others again, that is, we who are reckoned by the name of Christ, declare that they are being fulfilled daily in the Church, and will be fulfilled, until the end of the world.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference (Zech. 13:7). The text has 'C. Pompeium'; Pompey's praenomen was Gnaeus. 'ήλειμμένψ' read as ἠλειμμένῳ ('anointed'), i.e. their messiah.

passages.original: Hoc ipsum et Amos propheta ad Amasiam impium sacerdotem commi- nans loquitur : Uxor tua in civitate fornicabitur, et filii tui et filiae in gladio cadent, et humus tua funiculo metietur (AmosVII, 17). Et haec populo Judaeorum universa contingent : Quia fremuerunt gentes, et populi meditati sunt inania. Astiterunt reges terrae, et principes convenerunt in unum ad- versum Dominum et adversum Christum ejus (Psal.II, 1, 2). Qui irrisit et subsannavit eos, et in furore suo conturbavit illos, intantum ut Apostolus quo- que cernens eos annos qui ad poenitentiam dati fuerant, jam esse completos, et nihilominus illos in negatione persistere qui occiderunt Dominum, et prophetas et apostolos persecuti sunt, dixerit : Pervenit super eos [Al. nos] ira in finem (I Thess.II, 16). Haec omnia plenissime Josephus, qui Judai- cam scripsit historiam, et multo majora quam legimus in prophetis, eos sustinuisse commemo- rat. Cornelius quoque Tacitus, qui post Augustum usque ad mortem Domitiani Vitas 914 Caesarum triginta voluminibus exaravit.
passages.english: The prophet Amos also says this very thing, threatening Amaziah the impious priest: 'Your wife will play the harlot in the city, and your sons and daughters will fall by the sword, and your land will be measured by the line' (Amos 7:17). And all these things will befall the Jewish people, because 'the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things. The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ' (Ps. 2:1-2). He laughed at them and mocked them, and in his fury threw them into confusion, so much so that the Apostle too, seeing that the years which had been given for repentance were now completed, and that those who killed the Lord and persecuted the prophets and apostles nonetheless persisted in denial, said: 'Wrath has come upon them [another reading: us] to the end' (1 Thess. 2:16). All these things Josephus, who wrote the Jewish history, relates most fully, recording that they endured even far greater things than we read in the prophets. Cornelius Tacitus also, who after Augustus, up to the death of Domitian, wrote out the Lives of the Caesars in thirty volumes.
passages.notes: The last sentence is incomplete as it stands (no main verb); presumably 'relates the same' is understood, or the sentence continues beyond the passage.
